name: Jakob's Law
description: Users spend most of their time on other sites/products, so they prefer yours to work the way those already do.
design_relevance_note: One of the most commonly cited 'laws' in UX practice, used to justify following platform conventions.
myth_risk_note: No rigorous peer-reviewed empirical backing was found in the discovery data for this widely-taught UX principle. Jakob's Law is a well-known named principle in UX design practice and education, yet zero on-topic empirical papers were identified, suggesting either very limited formal validation or that validation does not appear in peer-reviewed academic literature.
prevalence_note: Jakob Nielsen's own principle ('users spend most of their time on other sites'), one of the most frequently cited UX heuristics in practice.

applications.title: Amazon's shopping-cart icon as an inherited convention
applications.description: The shopping-cart icon for e-commerce checkout, which Amazon is credited with popularizing in 1994, is now followed across essentially all e-commerce sites -- a convention followed because users already expect it from other sites, not because any one site tested and chose it independently.
applications.ethical_note: This is a clean, low-risk illustration of Jakob's Law: following an inherited convention purely to reduce user confusion, with no persuasion or urgency angle at all. Included specifically to show that a BiasHeuristic entry with no_rigorous_backing_found (Jakob's Law itself has none in this corpus) can still have a genuinely benign, well-documented practical application -- the lack of rigorous backing is about whether the general principle has been formally tested, not a signal that its applications are suspect.

applications.title: Centered vs. left-aligned logo placement and homepage-return failure rate
applications.description: A cited usability study found users failed to navigate back to the homepage substantially more often when a site's logo was centered rather than left-aligned, the conventional position -- presented as a direct cost of breaking from the expected layout convention Jakob's Law describes.
applications.ethical_note: Following the logo-placement convention is purely a usability accommodation with no persuasion angle -- the harm being described runs the other way, toward a business that breaks convention 'to appear unique' and costs its own users real navigation success. Flagging the excluded 80% claim here rather than silently dropping it, since that specific rejection is itself a direct, concrete demonstration of this methodology's checklist working as intended.
